paper_title: Mycelium: A Meta-Study of Hallucination Detection Across Provenance, Typology, and Granularities

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Hallucination detection is increasingly important for evaluating and deploying large language models. However, existing methods are often compared across benchmarks that define and measure hallucination in substantially different ways, making reported scores difficult to interpret across settings. We study hallucination detection as a benchmark-conditioned measurement problem and organize existing benchmarks along three axes: provenance, which describes how model outputs and evidence conditions are obtained; typology, which captures the factuality and faithfulness failures represented by benchmark labels; and granularity, which specifies the unit at which hallucinations are annotated, predicted, and evaluated. Using this framework, we analyze how benchmark construction, annotation, and evaluation choices shape the underlying prediction task, and relate detector mechanisms and assumptions to the settings in which their performance is measured. We also examine span-level evaluation, where variation in annotation boundaries can substantially affect reported results, and propose Span Coverage F1 as a complementary containment-based metric. Our analysis clarifies what detector scores capture, highlights limitations of cross-benchmark comparisons, and motivates more explicit evaluation of generalization across benchmark conditions.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Large language models (LLMs) achieve strong performance across wide range of natural language generation tasks and are increasingly integrated into larger AI systems (Yang et al., 2025; Guo et al., 2025; Singh et al., 2025). Despite these advances, they continue to hallucinate, producing fluent and plausible statements that are unsupported by available evidence, contradictory to given source, or inconsistent with established facts (Ji et al., 2023; Huang et al., 2025; Alansari and Luqman, 2026). The consequences of such errors extend beyond an individual model response. In retrieval-augmented generation, hallucinations appear as claims that are not grounded in the retrieved context (Niu et al., 2024; Friel et al., 2024; Es et al., 2024). In agentic and multi-agent systems, an unfaithful intermediate output may be passed to downstream tools, stored in memory, or reused by other agents, allowing local error to propagate into broader systemlevel failure (Gosmar and Dahl, 2025; Lin et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2025). Reliably identifying such outputs is therefore essential for the dependable deployment of LLM-based systems. Accordingly, hallucination detection has become an increasingly active research area, reflected in the growing number of dedicated benchmarks, shared tasks, and evaluation competitions (Min et al., 2023; Li et al., 2023; Vashurin et al., 2025; Mickus et al., 2024; Vázquez et al., 2025; Sinha et al., 2025). Existing approaches differ in both mechanism and output granularity, ranging from response-level LLM judges and alignmentbased factuality models to claim-level verification pipelines, span-level localizers, and multi-level systems that combine detection with localization, error typing, or correction. However, methods studied under the common label of hallucination detection are often trained and evaluated on substantially different prediction problems. claim-level evaluator such as FActScore (Min et al., 2023) or VeriScore (Song et al., 2024) does not address the same target as span-level detector evaluated on RAGTruth (Niu et al., 2024; Kovács and Recski, 2025), nor as response-level judge evaluated on HaluEval or SHROOM (Li et al., 2023; Mickus et al., 2024). In claim-level evaluation, the result depends on how response is decomposed into verifiable propositions and how their verdicts are aggregated; in span-level evaluation, on annotation boundaries and overlap metrics; and in response-level evaluation, on aggregation and decision protocols. Consequently, headline scores across these settings are not directly comparable, even when they are reported as measuring the same underlying phenomenon. Benchmark construction determines the error distribution, the distinctions exposed by the labels, and the signals available to detectors, thereby constraining the generalization claims supported by reported score. Natural, semi-natural, and synthetic benchmarks differ in how model outputs and evidence conditions are obtained, while binary and typed annotations expose different failure modes. These choices are not incidental: they operationalize what counts as hallucination and what detector is evaluated to recognize. Prior surveys provide broad taxonomies of hallucination causes, types, detection, evaluation, and mitigation (Ji et al., 2023; Huang et al., 2025). Evaluation-centered studies further organize existing evaluators by granularity, design, and assessment criteria (Qi et al., 2024). In contrast, we take detection benchmark-centered perspective: we examine how benchmarks operationalize hallucination and how these choices determine what detectors are evaluated to recognize. We therefore study hallucination detection as benchmark-conditioned measurement problem, structured along three axes: provenance, typology, and granularity (Figure 1). The code and all materials are publicly available at GitHub1. Our main contributions are: We introduce common analytical framework for hallucination detection structured around provenance, typology, and granularity. We provide comprehensive analysis of modern hallucination benchmarks, covering their construction, annotation protocols, evidence regimes, and evaluation metrics. We systematize hallucination detectors by relat1https://github.com/lmeribal/mycelium ing their mechanisms, access assumptions, and output units to the benchmark conditions under which their performance is measured. We empirically examine metric choice in spanlevel evaluation, showing how annotator boundary variation affects localization scores, and propose Span Coverage F1 as complementary metric for contained boundary refinements.

sections.title: 2 Scope and Formal Framework
sections.content: We treat hallucination as property of an evaluated configuration, comprising the input, generated output, available evidence, and evaluation unit, rather than as an intrinsic property of model. detector score therefore characterizes the interaction between method and the benchmark under which it is measured. Scope and evidence We consider textual LLM outputs containing declarative, truth-evaluable content. Hallucination detection concerns whether an error occurs, where it occurs, and, when supported by the annotation scheme, what type of error it represents. Mitigation and correction are included only when coupled with an explicit detection stage; internal model signals are in scope when used for detection, while causal analysis of hallucination mechanisms is outside our scope. Let denote an input, generated output, and the evidence available under benchmark. Evidence may consist of provided source C(x), retrieved material R(x), or time-indexed world-knowledge reference Wt. Relative to E, proposition may be supported, contradicted, or undetermined. Source faithfulness concerns support from C(x) or R(x), whereas factuality concerns consistency with Wt; consequently, content may be factually correct but unsupported by the designated context, or contextsupported but inconsistent with world knowledge. Analytical axes We characterize benchmarks along three dimensions. Granularity distinguishes four broad benchmark formulations: responselevel, span-level, claim-level, and multi-level. Provenance specifies whether hallucinations arise naturally from model outputs, are elicited under deliberately arranged conditions, or are constructed synthetically. Typology specifies the distinctions represented by benchmark labels, ranging from binary judgments to evidence-relation labels and task-specific error taxonomies. These choices determine the benchmarks prediction target and are Figure 1: Three analytical dimensions for hallucination detection: granularity, provenance, and typology. Existing benchmarks occupy different regions of this space, which explains why headline scores are often not directly comparable. analyzed in detail in Section 3. Benchmark-conditioned measurement Let benchmark = (D, p, g, L, λ, µ) comprise its instance distribution, provenance, granularity, label space, annotation rule, and evaluation metric. Here, DB is distribution over tuples (x, y, E, ℓ). detector has its own output representation, evidence requirements, and model-access assumptions. Its reported score is S(d; B) = E(x,y,E,ℓ)DB ˆℓ = ΠBd (cid:0)d(x, y, E)(cid:1), (cid:2)µB(ˆℓ, ℓ)(cid:3), (1) where ΠBd aligns the detector output with the representation required by the benchmark through operations such as thresholding, span projection, claim decomposition, or aggregation. Thus, S(d; B) characterizes the detectorbenchmark pair. Scores from different benchmarks are directly comparable only when their target semantics, granularities, label spaces, alignment procedures, metrics, and instance distributions are sufficiently compatible.

sections.title: 3 The Benchmark Landscape
sections.content: Equation 1 provides common view of how benchmark design affects detector evaluation. The three analytical axes act on different components of the measurement: granularity determines the target representation and detector-to-benchmark alignment ΠBd; provenance shapes the evaluation distribution DB; and typology determines the label space LB and annotation rule λB. These effects are distinct: detector may therefore receive different scores because it is evaluated on different instances, against different target, or through different representation and metric. We examine each source of variation in turn. 3.1 Granularity Granularity determines the unit over which hallucination is annotated, predicted, and evaluated. Figure 2 summarizes the benchmark inventory, distinguishing response-, span-, claim-, and multi-level formulations together with their typical metrics. In terms of Eq. 1, granularity determines the target representation gB and may also affect the detectorto-benchmark alignment ΠBd and evaluation metric µB. Consequently, similarly named scores can measure substantially different capabilities across granularities, and results should be interpreted with respect to the unit at which the underlying prediction problem is defined. Response-level Response-level benchmarks assign single judgment to the complete generation (Mickus et al., 2024; Sinha et al., 2025; Li et al., 2023; Friel et al., 2024; Jacovi et al., 2025; Oh et al., 2024). This formulation is suitable for overall factuality assessment, model comparFigure 2: Granularity of contemporary hallucination detection benchmarks. Resources use response-, span-, claim-, and multi-level formulations; span-level benchmarks further vary in character-, word-, entity-, and sentenceresolution. Each formulation supports different evaluation objectives and metrics. ison, and output filtering, but it does not reveal where an error occurs or how much of the response is affected. Accuracy, F1, AUROC, correlation, and aggregate grounding scores therefore evaluate whole-output discrimination rather than localization. When detector produces finer-grained predictions, response-level evaluation additionally depends on how these predictions are aggregated through ΠBd. Span-level Span-level benchmarks localize hallucinated content using character-level, wordor token-level, entity-level, or sentence-level spans (Vázquez et al., 2025; Niu et al., 2024; Yeh et al., 2025; Ji et al., 2024; Sadat et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2026). These formulations differ both in unit size and in what constitutes localized error. Characterand token-level annotations emphasize boundary precision, entity-level annotations group text into semantically meaningful mentions, and sentence-level annotations provide coarser units that may merge several local factual judgments. Span-level results must therefore be interpreted together with the annotation unit. Even within fixed span type, however, the reference annotation need not define unique localization target. Annotators may mark minimal erroneous phrase, the complete factual unit containing it, or broader expression that captures the same unsupported content. Mu-SHROOM (Vázquez et al., 2025) makes this variation observable by retaining multiple span annotations for the same outputs. Span-level evaluation therefore involves two distinct choices: the unit in which hallucination is represented and the relation between prediction and reference that the metric treats as correct. We examine the latter separately in Section 3.2. Claim-level Claim-level benchmarks evaluate independently verifiable factual units (Min et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2023). Their scores depend both on verification outcomes and on how the generation is decomposed. Atomicity, claim scope, decontextualization, and verifiability filtering determine which units are evaluated and, in aggregate metrics, the score denominator. In the formulation of Eq. 1, decomposition therefore becomes part of the effective alignment ΠBd. Claim-level results produced under different decomposition policies are consequently not directly interchangeable even when they use similar verification metrics. Multi-level Multi-level benchmarks connect several targets, such as detecting an error, localizing it, assigning an error type, and evaluating correction (Mishra et al., 2024). They provide more actionable diagnosis than single annotation level but require separate metrics for the capabilities being assessed. single scalar score may otherwise conflate localization, classification, and correction quality. Across all four granularities, benchmark comparisons should therefore account for the annotation unit, any transformation between detector and benchmark outputs, and the metric that defines agreement between prediction and reference. Spanlevel evaluation introduces an additional complication because the boundaries of localized error may themselves be non-unique. We next examine this measurement problem and introduce metric designed to capture one particular invariance to Figure 3: Effect of annotation variation within the span-level family. The same detector prediction is evaluated against character-, word-, entity-, and sentence-level annotations using their corresponding metrics. such boundary variation. 3.2 Span Coverage F1: Evaluation under Boundary Variation Span localization requires an evaluation rule for determining when predicted region and an annotated region refer to the same error. This choice becomes consequential when annotations admit multiple plausible boundaries. prediction may identify the correct erroneous content while selecting narrower phrase than the reference, whereas another prediction may extend beyond the annotated error while still substantially overlapping it. Metrics differ in whether and how they distinguish these cases. Existing evaluation semantics We compare six metrics spanning four evaluation semantics. Exact span F1 treats annotated spans as fixed instances and rewards only identical boundaries. Character F1 and character IoU collapse spans into character masks and measure graded textual overlap, making them less sensitive to exact boundaries but largely insensitive to how the covered text is partitioned into instances. We additionally consider one-dimensional adaptations of DetEval (Wolf and Jolion, 2006) and CLEval (Baek et al., 2020), denoted DetEval-1D and CLEval-1D. These metrics were originally designed for two-dimensional text regions and explicitly accommodate one-to-many and many-to-one correspondences. Together, these baselines provide controls for exact instance agreement, mask overlap, and splitmerge-aware matching. whose size equals the number of included character positions. Accordingly, two-dimensional intersection area is replaced by interval-intersection length. For DetEval-1D, the resulting overlap measures are ℓ([s, e]) = + 1, σij = Iij gi , Iij = gi pj, Iij pj τij = . (2) One-to-one matches require at least 80% coverage of the reference span and at least 40% coverage of the predicted span. For one-to-many match, every participating prediction must satisfy the latter condition, while their combined overlap must cover at least 80% of the reference. Many-to-one matches use the corresponding reverse conditions. Matching is performed in one-to-one, one-to-many, and many-to-one order. One-to-one matches receive unit credit, while accepted splits and merges receive credit of 0.8 for each participating instance. For CLEval-1D, every character offset within reference span is treated as pseudo-character center, and the original area-precision threshold of 0.3 is applied using interval overlap. Precision and recall are based on the number of uniquely covered reference characters. Each additional prediction matched to the same reference subtracts one character from the recall credit; correspondingly, each additional reference matched to the same prediction subtracts one character from the precision credit. Because character-span lengths are observed directly, the aspect-ratio estimate used for two-dimensional prediction boxes is replaced by the exact predicted interval length. For both one-dimensional adaptations, each inclusive character span is treated as an interval These formulations accommodate different forms of boundary disagreement, but none directly represents another plausible semantics of hallucination localization: detector may identify more specific erroneous phrase that lies fully within broader annotated hallucinated region. This case is especially relevant when the annotation is not assumed to identify unique minimal boundary. Span Coverage F1 To represent this relation, we propose Span Coverage F1, an instance-level containment metric. Let and denote the sets of predicted and reference spans, respectively. Prediction coverage measures the proportion of predicted spans that are fully contained in at least one reference span, while reference coverage measures the proportion of reference spans that contain at least one predicted span: Pcov = Rcov = (cid:12){ : G, }(cid:12) (cid:12) (cid:12) (cid:12){ : P, }(cid:12) (cid:12) (cid:12) . , (3) We combine the two quantities using their harmonic mean: Span Coverage F1 = 2PcovRcov Pcov + Rcov . (4) Span Coverage F1 is intentionally directional. narrower prediction contained within broader reference is treated as successful localization, whereas prediction extending beyond the annotated region is not. Unlike character-mask metrics, it operates on span instances and therefore preserves whether individual annotated regions have been localized. Unlike exact span matching, it is invariant to inward boundary refinements. Its semantics also differ from graded overlap metrics, which penalize inward and outward deviations according to the amount of shared text. The metric therefore encodes specific assumption: when an annotation provides an admissible hallucinated region rather than unique minimal boundary, detector should not necessarily be penalized for identifying more specific subspan within that region. Span Coverage F1 is intended to test this containment semantics and is complementary to overlap-sensitive measures. Experimental setup We study these alternatives using the English Mu-SHROOM test set (Vázquez et al., 2025). The analysis contains 154 examples and 1,665 annotator-level span sets. Among 6,280 non-empty, non-identical annotation pairs, 1,403 (22.3%) are boundary-nested while preserving the same number of connected components. These cases provide an observable proxy for boundary variation: the annotations localize overlapping content with different extents, without requiring either annotator to define the uniquely correct boundary. We further perform leave-one-annotator-out (LOO) evaluation. For each example, one annotators span set is treated as the prediction, while the remaining annotators define the reference using either strict character-level majority or their union. Majority produces narrower consensus region, whereas union forms broader envelope containing every character selected by at least one remaining annotator. These constructions are not treated as alternative gold standards. Instead, they expose how the same held-out localization is scored as the admissible reference extent changes. The 1-Char diagnostic retains only 3.1% of reference characters on average. Results Under LOO evaluation, Span Coverage F1 increases from 0.410 with the majority reference to 0.750 with the broader union, consistent with its invariance to contained refinements. Exact span F1 moves in the opposite direction (0.288 to 0.071), as the broader reference rarely preserves identical boundaries. DetEval-1D also decreases (0.574 to 0.239) because it requires substantial reference coverage, while character F1, character IoU, and CLEval-1D change more moderately. The same qualitative pattern holds under micro aggregation: Span Coverage F1 rises from 0.369 to 0.713, DetEval-1D falls from 0.534 to 0.198, and character IoU remains nearly unchanged (0.455 versus 0.461). The relation-specific analysis clarifies these differences. On the nested-boundary subset, Span Coverage F1 assigns full credit by construction: each held-out prediction is contained in the broader reference, with the same number of connected spans. The same cases score 0.281 under DetEval1D, 0.605 under CLEval-1D and character F1, 0.503 under character IoU, and 0.032 under exact span F1. Span Coverage F1 falls to 0.347 for partial overlaps and to zero for disjoint annotations. Its high nested-boundary score thus reflects containment specifically, rather than general tolerance for spatial disagreement. Overall, the same localization receives different scores because the metrics encode different invariances. They answer distinct evaluation questions rather than forming simple scale from stricter to more permissive. Limitations and complementary use Containment deliberately ignores how much of reference span is recovered. In the 1-Char stress test, predicting one character inside each reference span covers only 3.1% of reference characters but achieves Span Coverage F1 = 1.000; character IoU is 0.031. perfect containment score can therefore indicate that every annotated region was touched without indicating that its full extent was localized. Span Coverage F1 should be interpreted as an instance-level containment measure and reported alongside an overlap-sensitive metric, such as character F1 or character IoU, when localization extent matters. Together, the scores show whether predictions lie within annotated regions and how much of those regions they cover. 3.3 Provenance Provenance describes how hallucinated content enters benchmark and is independent of how it is subsequently annotated. We distinguish natural, semi-natural, and synthetic provenance. The distinction matters because benchmark construction determines the error distribution: natural data reflects failures produced under the task setting, seminatural data amplifies failures through deliberately arranged conditions, and synthetic data reflects the perturbation or generation procedure used to create errors. Natural benchmarks collect model outputs produced under the intended task setting and identify hallucinations after generation (Niu et al., 2024; Mickus et al., 2024; Pagnoni et al., 2021; Yeh et al., 2025). The benchmark does not predetermine which error should occur; hallucinated content arises from the interaction between the generator, task, domain, and available evidence. Natural provenance is therefore closer to deployment-like behavior, but its error rates and forms are harder to control and may vary substantially across models and settings. Semi-natural benchmarks retain genuine modelgenerated errors but deliberately modify or select the generation conditions to make hallucination more likely. PsiloQA withholds context required to answer the questions, inducing unsupported generation without directly inserting errors (Rykov et al., 2025). HaluEval-Wild instead selects real user queries that are likely to trigger failures (Zhu et al., 2024). Such benchmarks support controlled stress-testing, but their distributions overrepresent failure modes associated with the induced condition and should not be treated as unbiased task data. Synthetic benchmarks create hallucinations or adverse evidence conditions directly. HADES perturbs source text, FAVA-Bench injects controlled factual errors, FaithEval constructs inconsistent, unanswerable, and counterfactual contexts, and HaluEval generates and filters hallucinated responses (Liu et al., 2022; Mishra et al., 2024; Ming et al., 2024; Li et al., 2023). This design enables targeted coverage and class balancing, but the resulting distribution may reflect construction artifacts. Performance on synthetic data therefore does not necessarily transfer to naturally occurring model failures. 3.4 Typology Typology specifies which hallucination categories benchmark distinguishes. Figure 2 summarizes three broad regimes. Binary and coarse typologies indicate only the presence or degree of hallucination; evidence-relation typologies characterize generated content through its support status with respect to available evidence; and task-specific taxonomies distinguish particular factual, linguistic, discourse, or reasoning failures. Typology is orthogonal to granularity and provenance: benchmarks may evaluate the same textual unit and obtain examples through similar procedures while defining substantially different labels. Binary benchmarks collapse heterogeneous failures into single hallucinated versus nonhallucinated decision, as in SHROOM and HaluEval (Mickus et al., 2024; Li et al., 2023). Coarse typologies retain limited notion of severity: WikiBio-GPT3 distinguishes Accurate, Minor Inaccurate, and Major Inaccurate sentences, while PHD ultimately distinguishes factual from nonfactual passages (Manakul et al., 2023; Yang et al., 2023). Such labels support filtering and aggregate Figure 4: Taxonomy of hallucination detectors by model access, signal source, detection mechanism, output granularity, and proxy transferability. Representative methods are listed in the final column. comparison, but they make contradiction, unsupported addition, entity substitution, and invalid inference observationally equivalent. Evidence-relation typologies preserve how generated content relates to reference or knowledge source. RAGTruth distinguishes Evident Conflict, Subtle Conflict, Evident Baseless Information, and Subtle Baseless Information, jointly encoding the relation to the context and how explicit the error is (Niu et al., 2024). ANAH uses No Hallucination, Contradictory Hallucination, Unverifiable Hallucination, and No Fact, separating unsupported factual statements from sentences without checkable factual content (Ji et al., 2024). At claim level, FActScore labels atomic facts as supported or unsupported, whereas FactCheckBench additionally distinguishes whether unit is check-worthy and whether retrieved evidence completely supports, partially supports, refutes, or is irrelevant to the claim (Min et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2024). FaithBench further incorporates acceptability: hallucinations may be Questionable, Benign, or Unwanted, with the last category divided into Intrinsic contradictions and Extrinsic unsupported and non-factual additions (Bao et al., 2025). Task-specific taxonomies describe the form through which an error manifests. FRANK groups summarization errors into three families (Pagnoni et al., 2021). Semantic-frame errors include Predicate, Entity, and Circumstance; discourse errors include Coreference and Discourse Link; and content-verifiability errors include Out-of-Article and Grammatical. FAVA-Bench distinguishes Entity, Relation, Contradictory, Invented, Subjective, and Unverifiable errors (Mishra et al., 2024). TofuEval adapts the taxonomy to dialogue summarization with Extrinsic Information, Mis-Referencing, Stating Opinion as Fact, Reasoning Error, Tense/- Modality Error, Contradiction, and Nuanced Meaning Shift (Tang et al., 2024). FELM distinguishes Knowledge, Reasoning, Irrelevant, and Fooled errors, while DiaHalu uses Non-factual, Incoherence, Irrelevance, Overreliance, and Reasoning Error for multi-turn dialogue (Chen et al., 2023, 2024). HILT uses multidimensional scheme that combines factual-mirage versus silver-lining orientation, intrinsic versus extrinsic status, three severity levels, and six descriptive categories covering numeric, temporal, geographic, attribution-related, and other errors (Rawte et al., 2023). Despite different names, several recurring correspondences appear across these taxonomies. Conflict-like errors include RAGTruth Conflict, ANAH Contradictory Hallucination, FaithBench Unwanted Intrinsic, FAVA-Bench Contradictory, and TofuEval Contradiction. Unsupported additions include RAGTruth Baseless Information, FActScore Unsupported, FaithBench Unwanted Extrinsic, FRANK Out-of-Article, TofuEval Extrinsic Information, and FAVA-Bench Invented or Unverifiable. Local semantic errors similarly connect FAVA-Bench entity and relation errors with FRANK entity, predicate, and circumstance errors, while discourse and reasoning failures recur in FRANK, TofuEval, FELM, and DiaHalu. These correspondences are many-to-many rather than exact equivalences: their meaning depends on the task, evidence regime, and annotation rules. Benchmark comparisons should therefore account for both the category definitions and their empirical distributions.

sections.title: 4 The Detector Landscape
sections.content: Figure 4 organizes hallucination detectors along four operational dimensions: the required access to the generator, the signal used for detection, the output granularity, and the possibility of transferring the detector through separate inspector model. In the formulation of Eq. 1, these dimensions characterize the native detector d(x, y, E) and, where necessary, the alignment ΠBd required to evaluate it under benchmark. The figure provides the method-level inventory; here we focus on the main trade-offs that follow from these dimensions. 4.1 Access and Signal Source Black-box detectors operate on textual inputs and outputs. They include direct LLM judges, decomposition-and-verification pipelines, sourcealignment models, supervised text classifiers, and sampling-based consistency methods (Liu et al., 2023; Min et al., 2023; Zha et al., 2023; Manakul et al., 2023). Their main advantage is portability: they can be applied to closed models without access to logits or activations. This portability may come at the cost of external judge calls, retrieval, or repeated generation. Evidence access also varies within this family. Some methods are reference-free and infer unreliability from disagreement or self-consistency, whereas others compare the output with fixed context or retrieve external evidence. In terms of Eq. 1, these methods therefore differ in the information from available to d(x, y, E). These settings should not be conflated, since consistency is only an indirect proxy for factual support. White-box detectors instead use generator-side uncertainty, hidden representations, attention patterns, or geometric properties of the activation space (Kuhn et al., 2023; Azaria and Mitchell, 2023; Chuang et al., 2024; Yin et al., 2024). Such signals may reveal failures that are not evident from the output alone, but they require access to an open model and are often tied to particular architecture, layer, or checkpoint. 4.2 Output Granularity and Transfer Detector output granularities follow the benchmark units introduced in Section 3.1. When detector and benchmark granularities differ, this mismatch is represented by ΠBd in Eq. 1. Transfer across these units is asymmetric: localized predictions can usually be aggregated into sentenceor responselevel scores, whereas response-level decision cannot be converted into faithful spans or claims without an additional localization or decomposition stage. For claim-level detectors, decomposition is part of the detection procedure rather than neutral preprocessing. Atomicity, decontextualization, verifiability filtering, and claim representation determine which units are verified and the denominator of the resulting score (Min et al., 2023; Wei et al., 2024; Song et al., 2024; Hu et al., 2024; Metropolitansky and Larson, 2025). These operations therefore form part of the effective alignment between the detector output and the benchmark target in ΠBd. Claim-level results may consequently conflate extraction and verification quality. Projecting claim verdicts onto fixed sentence-level unit can reduce extractor-induced variation in cross-method comparisons, although it sacrifices some localization fidelity. Transferability also concerns the source of whitebox signals. Uncertainty estimates generally require probabilities from the original generator, whereas some representationand geometry-based detectors can operate through separate openweight inspector model. Because proxy inspection replaces the generators internal signal with that of another model, it changes the signal underlying d(x, y, E) and should be reported explicitly rather than treated as equivalent to direct generator access. 4.3 Supervision and Calibration Supervision cuts across the taxonomy in Figure 4. Prompted judges and sampling-based methods may require no detector training. Uncertainty scores typically require threshold calibration. Hiddenstate probes use smaller labeled set to fit lightweight classifier, and fine-tuned text or span detectors require substantially more task-specific supervision (Farquhar et al., 2024; Azaria and Mitchell, 2023; Zha et al., 2023; Kovács and Recski, 2025). Increasing supervision often improves in-distribution accuracy but reduces portability across models, domains, granularities, and label definitions. In Eq. 1, thresholding, aggregation, and other benchmark-specific decision procedures are included in ΠBd. Comparisons should therefore report the supervision source, calibration protocol, and aggregation rule together with the final detector score.

sections.title: 5 Conclusion
sections.content: This meta-study shows that hallucination detection results are inseparable from the benchmarks on which they are obtained. Differences in how hallucinations are generated, categorized, localized, and scored determine what detector is evaluated to recognize and what its reported performance represents. Our span-level metric analysis makes this dependence concrete: the same localization can receive substantially different evaluations depending on whether correctness is defined through exact boundaries, graded overlap, or containment. Multiannotator Mu-SHROOM data further show that boundary-nested disagreement is common enough to make this choice practically relevant. By jointly characterizing benchmarks through provenance, typology, and granularity, and detectors through their outputs, access assumptions, evidence requirements, mechanisms, and supervision, we provide common basis for interpreting existing results. Span Coverage F1 illustrates one possible measurement semantics for non-unique span boundaries by accepting contained refinements, while its stress-test failure demonstrates why no single metric captures all aspects of localization quality. More generally, evaluation should make explicit which variations in annotation are intended to be invariant and which constitute detector errors. Future work should therefore move beyond higher in-benchmark scores toward controlled evaluation of detector robustness across data construction, error type, annotation unit, and metric semantics.
